parts.title: A workable model of how memories are stored, using chance and networks of nerve cells
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Long-term memory seems to hold an enormous amount of information, enough to cover almost a whole lifetime. Why is it so big? Why do some memories last so long? And what does a long-term memory actually look like inside the brain? In the movie Inside Out, each memory is shown as a small glowing ball holding a piece of information. Is that really how it works?

The cortex, the outer layer of the brain, has a huge number of nerve cells (neurons), a huge number of connections between them, and complicated electrical and chemical activity going on between them. But simply pointing to these facts does not answer the basic questions. We need to uncover the theory that lies behind them.

To do this, we treat a network of nerve cells as a very large directed graph. A directed graph is a map of points, called nodes, joined by arrows that point in one direction. Here, each node is a nerve cell, and each arrow is a connection that sends a signal from one cell to another. We propose that a long-term memory is a connected subgraph inside this huge graph. A connected subgraph is a smaller group of nodes that are all linked together, so you can travel from any one of them to any other by following the arrows.

This connected subgraph can join together the scattered pieces of the same event, which are stored in different parts of the cortex that handle different senses, and link them into a single memory. This gives a physical form to the engram theory, the idea that each memory is stored as a lasting mark in the brain. How sturdy this connected subgraph is, and how much of the brain's resources it uses, can explain many of the ways memory behaves.

Using evidence from brain anatomy, brain imaging and recordings of electrical activity in the brain, we build a model of how likely two nerve cells are to be connected. We then use theorems from graph theory, the mathematics of networks, to prove that connected subgraphs are easy to form. Finally, we explain why the brain could hold an immense amount of memory.

Keywords: capacity, directed graph, engram theory, long-term memory, probability model
parts.introduction_first:
We know exactly how much information a 1 TB hard drive can hold. How much information a piece of cortex, the outer layer of the brain, can hold is a very different story.

Digital files such as photos or text are stored in physical forms that we understand well. A photo sits on a hard drive, or in the tiny floating gate of a solid-state drive, a small charged region that holds a bit of data. These devices are carefully designed to carry information. For the brain, though, we still cannot measure how much it stores.

We can ask deep questions: "What form does a piece of information take in the brain?", "How many resources does storing one piece of information use?", and "How are those resources shared out?" For mechanical storage devices, we understand every step of how information is turned into a physical form. For the brain, the key details of how meaning-based memory (semantic memory) or memory of events (episodic memory) is physically built remain hazy.
parts.introduction_rest:
The memory system has three core jobs: storage, consolidation and retrieval. Together they make it a system for handling information. It holds on to information, and that information changes how we act in the future. Storage means forming memories. It works by encoding, which is turning what we experience into a form the brain can keep, so that we can find it again later. Consolidation makes memories last longer, so they survive until we need them much later. Retrieval means bringing stored information back to life using clues, so that we can recall something or recognize it. Scientists have built ideas about how the memory system is organized from tests of behavior. These tests led to the multi-store memory model proposed by Atkinson (1968), which pictures memory as information passing through several stores.

Episodic memory, the memory of events, is a typical example of long-term memory. It gathers information about events through many senses: sight, hearing, touch, smell, taste and the sense of where things are in space. When one particular clue is triggered, the whole setting of the event comes back.

Research on context-dependent memory, meaning memory that depends on the setting, shows this clearly. Baddeley and Godden ran tests in which they changed the setting between the time people learned something and the time they were asked to remember it. People did better when they were in a setting similar to the one they had learned in (Godden and Baddeley, 1975). This suggested that a setting like the learning setting helps us retrieve information, and that the many sides of an event are encoded together.

How does this work? The Contextual Binding Model offers an explanation. It proposes that when a memory is first handled by the hippocampus, a brain region deep inside the brain that is important for memory, the areas that recognize "what" an object is and "where" it is connect to the hippocampus (Yonelinas et al., 2019). However, this explanation is still too vague to describe in detail how a memory is physically laid out.

Besides studying behavior, neuroscience has also studied memory in great detail, and the engram theory is one of its current hot topics. The word "engram" was first proposed by Richard Semon in 1911. At first it meant changes in the brain caused by things outside the body that have long-lasting effects (Semon, 1925). In modern neuroscience experiments, the engram is mostly described in terms of the body's physical responses.

Classic studies of engram cells suggest that an engram first forms in the hippocampus and then gradually moves to the mPFC (medial prefrontal cortex), a region at the front of the brain, during consolidation. Once a long-term memory engram is firmly set, it is brought back to life when nerve signals travel along a route from the mPFC to the BLA (basolateral amygdala), a region that handles emotions such as fear, and this switches on the matching responses in the body. For example, in contextual fear conditioning, where mice learn to fear a particular setting after a shock, the strength of a mouse's shock response to the learned signal matches the activity of the engram in the BLA (Josselyn and Tonegawa, 2020; Kitamura et al., 2017; Tonegawa et al., 2018).

Other experiments have looked at the engram as a whole group of nerve cells working together, called an ensemble. They found that when one particular engram route is switched on, many smaller ensembles in different brain regions are switched on too, and similar patterns appear during slow wave sleep, the deep, restful stage of sleep (Roy et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023). This suggests that a particular engram is not only physically laid out in one ensemble in the hippocampus or BLA, but spreads across different parts of the whole brain. The ensembles in the hippocampus, BLA or mPFC may act as hubs that set off the whole engram map, so that we can recall the stored details (Roy et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023).

The connections between engram cells also differ from those between other nerve cells. The synapses, the contact points where one nerve cell passes a signal to another, differ in their shape and in how they work. This may show that the shape of the connections reflects how easily a memory can be retrieved (Choi et al., 2021; Hayashi-Takagi et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2023a,b). Taken together, this biological evidence pushes us toward a believable theory that points the way.

Marr's theory gives us a powerful set of tools for studying memory as a system that handles information (Marr, 1982). It suggests that any information system can be described at three levels: computation, algorithm and implementation. The results of behavior experiments fit the computational level, which shows what memory does. Methods from neurobiology, such as MRI, EEG (recordings of electrical activity in the brain), studies of the body's responses, or studies of molecules, may serve as the physical implementation. The algorithm level, the step-by-step rules that turn one level into the next, remains unclear. It is the missing link between the large-scale level and the small-scale level.

Studying how memory works at the level of behavior can be too broad, while studying it at the level of synapses and molecules can be too detailed. If we treat a network of nerve cells as a very large directed graph, encoding, consolidation and retrieval of events can be seen as forming, strengthening and switching on a connected subgraph inside that graph. This approach acts as a bridge that links the whole chain of how memory works. By modeling how likely nerve cells are to be connected, and by using mathematics to show that connected circuits exist, we can reveal the enormous capacity of biological networks of nerve cells in terms of large connected subgraphs. This could explain things like how much memory can hold, how long it lasts, and how we forget.

Directed graphs from graph theory may serve as a middle-level tool that connects the details of nerve cells with what we observe in behavior. We can think of this network, spread out across many parts of the brain, as the algorithm level. In this picture, the complicated electrical and chemical reactions between nerve cells become interactions between the nodes of the directed graph. Engrams can then be seen as a connected subgraph inside the directed graph that stands for one particular event.

In this picture, encoding a memory seems to involve forming such a connected subgraph. During consolidation, synapses get stronger, which matches the strengthening of the arrows in the graph and makes the subgraph more stable. Retrieval then means switching on the subgraphs stored earlier. This approach is fundamentally different from using graphs to study how regions of the cortex are functionally connected. In that kind of study, the nodes are regions of the cortex or of the brain below it, the arrows show connections linked to an event, and the results of graph calculations are taken as showing how relevant the regions are.

In studies of brain networks, five models that build undirected graphs, where arrows have no direction, are often used: ER random graphs, WS small-world networks, scale-free networks, spatial models and stochastic block models (Lynn and Bassett, 2019).

Spatial models place the nerve cells at their real positions in the brain. However, they do not capture how different brain regions interact and pass information to each other over time. In contrast, small-world networks, ER random graphs, scale-free networks and stochastic block models differ significantly from data collected in clinical experiments. One difference is that in real brain networks, the number of arrows pointing into a cell is often not the same as the number pointing out of it. Taking this into account, researchers have proposed that the chance of two nerve cells being connected drops exponentially as the distance between them grows, meaning it shrinks very quickly as distance increases (Horvát et al., 2016; Perin et al., 2011; Pillai et al., 2012). Meanwhile, Kramer compared models that build undirected graphs with clinical data on nerve cells in the amygdala, and found significant differences between the two (Kramer, 2023).

To conclude, we aim to develop a way of building directed graphs that matches the details of neurobiology, with directed subgraphs standing for engrams in the brain. By studying how these connected subgraphs can reach one another, tell one another apart, and exist side by side, we can offer a believable estimate of how much memory can hold.
parts.methods:
## 3. Methods

### 3.1. A mathematical model of how likely two nerve cells are to be connected

We started from the synaptic density field. This is a map of how crowded with synapses each part of the cortex is. A synapse is the spot where one nerve cell passes a signal to another. From this map we worked out how many synapses link any two nerve cells. From that count we then wrote down a formula for the connection probability between two nerve cells, meaning how likely they are to be connected. This formula is Equation 4. The Supplementary material gives the full details in the section "Neuron Connection Probability Modeling".

### 3.2. Building directed graphs that fit what we know about the brain

We used our model of how likely two nerve cells are to be connected as the starting point for building directed graphs. We then tested how well connected these graphs were, using graphs with different numbers of nodes. We judged this with three measures. Reachability tells us how many pairs of nodes can reach each other by following the arrows. Average path length tells us how many arrows you usually need to travel from one node to another. The clustering coefficient tells us how often a node's neighbours are also linked to each other, which shows how tightly knit a group is.

Graphs with 500 nodes were the best connected of all. So we chose a directed graph with 500 nodes for all the experiments that followed. The Supplementary material gives the details in the section "Modeling Directed Graphs that Meet Biological Constraints".

### 3.3. How the average one-way connection saturation of a subgraph depends on its size

Next, we set two settings of the directed graph, called k and λ, to k = 0.06 and λ = 41. We then took groups of nodes of different sizes from the graph and measured their average unidirectional connection saturation. This is the average share of all possible one-way links between the nodes in a group that actually exist. We used statistics to study how this share changes as the groups get bigger.

The experiment confirmed that once a group of nodes reaches a certain size, its average connection saturation settles at a fixed value. The Supplementary material gives the details in the section "Experiment on the Relationship Between the Average Unidirectional Connection Saturation of Directed Graph Subgraphs and Subgraph Size".

### 3.4. Counting Hamiltonian cycles in directed graphs

A Hamiltonian cycle is a loop that visits every node exactly once and then comes back to where it started. When a graph has only a few nodes, we counted its Hamiltonian cycles by having a computer try every possible loop. When a graph has many more nodes, we used the Monte Carlo method instead. This method makes a very large number of random guesses and uses the share that work to estimate the answer.

The experiment showed that both methods gave roughly the same results. Figure 3d shows the results. The Supplementary material gives the details in the section "Counting Hamiltonian Cycles in Directed Graphs".
parts.results:
## 2. Results

### 2.1. Memory marks are basically connected subgraphs

In neuroscience, the nerve cells that switch on and take part in storing a particular memory while it is being formed are called engram cells. To represent an event, the brain often needs a large number of these cells. Some of them sit in areas that handle different senses, so they are spread far apart, and they are joined together by certain connecting units.

This is like a connected subgraph in graph theory. If we think of the network of nerve cells as a very large, highly connected directed graph with no central hub, then each engram cell is one node in that graph. When these nodes are linked, they form a connected subgraph inside the huge directed graph of the brain. This connected subgraph could be the physical form of a memory mark.

Several connected subgraphs can exist side by side in the same network. They can share some of the same nodes, and they may lose some of their branches because they compete for the brain's resources. This physical form can fully explain how the brain carries out the three steps of memory: encoding (turning an experience into a memory), consolidation (locking the memory in place) and retrieval (bringing the memory back). It can also account for the conclusions drawn from experiments on memory in psychology.

### 2.2. A model of how likely nerve cells are to be connected

Any description of how a directed graph is connected has to be backed up by experiments on the brain. In brain anatomy, scientists have seen that short-range connections between nerve cells are more common than long-range ones. But this is not precise enough to build large directed graphs that come close to real networks of nerve cells. Real networks are not simple, free-form directed graphs. Their patterns of connection have to match what actually happens in the brain, at least on average.

To treat a network of nerve cells as a very large directed graph, we first need to set the rules for how each node connects to the others. Nerve cells connect to each other through synapses, the tiny contact points where one cell passes a signal to another. Suppose that whether a synapse forms between two cells at a particular spot in space is an independent event, meaning it does not depend on other events. And suppose that two nerve cells have enough synapses within a small enough neighbourhood. Then it is possible for these two cells to form synapses within that neighbourhood (Tecuatl et al., 2021).

Building on these findings from brain anatomy and from recordings of electrical activity, we worked out a model of how likely two nerve cells are to be connected. The model reflects what happens in the brain, and we checked that its settings agree with anatomical evidence. The chance that two nerve cells are connected depends on the distance between them.

Working this out (the details are in the Supplementary material: Neuron Connection Probability Modeling), we found that the number of synapses, N(d), formed between two nerve cells a distance d apart depends on several things. These are the distance d between the two cells; the distance r from the spot where a synapse forms to the soma, the main body of the cell; a constant A, which stands for the share of synapses on the sending side and the receiving side that are likely to connect within a very small neighbourhood; the synaptic density ρ0, which is how crowded with synapses the centre of the ellipsoid (a stretched ball-shaped region) is; and the synaptic density decay rate λ, which describes how quickly that crowding thins out with distance. Table 1 defines all the symbols in the equations. This gives Equation 1:

Table 1

Settings of the model.

| Symbol | Meaning

| d | The distance between the two nerve cells

| r | The distance from the spot where a synapse forms to the soma (the main body of the cell)

| ρ0 | The synaptic density at the centre of the ellipsoid

| A | The share of synapses on the sending side and the receiving side that are likely to connect within a very small neighbourhood

| λ | The synaptic density decay rate

| N(d) | The number of synapses formed between two nerve cells a distance d apart

| P(X = n) | The chance that a pair of nerve cells forms X synapse connections

(1) N(d) = Aρ0² ∑ e^(−2(r² + (d − r)²)λ) Δr

The chance that two nerve cells are connected depends on how many synapses lie between them. Research has shown that the Poisson distribution, a standard way of describing how often something happens when each chance is small and independent, fits the link between the possible number of synapses and the chance that two nerve cells are connected (Kersen et al., 2022). The chance that a pair of nerve cells forms x synapse connections is:

(2) P(x = n) = (N(d))^n / n! × e^(−N(d))

In real life, two nerve cells can have several synapses between them. For example, the end of the sending cell's axon (the long arm that carries signals away) can connect to many different parts of the receiving cell. These include the soma, the far or near ends of its dendrites (the branches that receive signals), or the axon hillock, the spot where the axon begins. In the directed graph model in this paper, we count all these synapses as a single arrow. So the chance that two nerve cells are connected is the chance that they have at least one synapse between them, which is the chance that the number of synapses is not zero:

(3) P(be_connected) = P(x ≠ 0) = 1 − P(x = 0) = 1 − (N(d))^0 / 0! × e^(−N(d)) = 1 − e^(−N(d)) = 1 − e^(−Aρ0² ∑ e^(−2(r² + ((d − r))²)λ) Δr)

Let k = Aρ0². Then:

(4) P(be_connected) = 1 − e^(−k ∑ e^(−2(r² + (d − r)²)λ) Δr)

Next, we need to find which settings produce a directed graph that matches what happens in the brain. For our later experiments, we chose a directed graph with 500 nodes (the reason for choosing 500 is given in the Supplementary material: Modeling Directed Graphs that Meet Biological Constraints). By trying different values of k and λ, we could imitate the different chances of connection between cells that have been seen in various experiments. Figure 1a compares our results with data from Budd and Kisvárday (2001), and Figure 1b compares them with data from Horvát et al. (2016). These comparisons show that our settings agree with real experimental data. This agreement confirms the settings, so we can use them in our later simulations of directed graphs.

Figure 1

The curve showing how likely two nerve cells are to be connected, depending on their distance. The yellow curve is our model and the green curve is data measured in experiments. (a) k = 0.06, λ = 41, compared with Budd's data. (b) k = 0.15, λ = 55, compared with Horvát's data.

### 2.3. The mathematics guarantees that memory marks can exist

A connected subgraph can be the physical form of a memory mark, as long as the directed graph has enough room. That means it can hold enough connected subgraphs that exist side by side without clashing. Also, the nerve cells switched on by a particular event are spread throughout the cortex, and they should be linked to each other fairly often. If a group of nodes has several different ways of being connected, then it is easy to make sure they are all linked.

Graph theory has a useful idea here. A Hamiltonian cycle is a path that visits every node in a graph and then returns to where it started. The same idea can be applied to a smaller group of nodes inside a directed graph. Hefetz et al. (2016) and Ferber et al. (2018) proved the following for a random directed graph D(N, p). Here N is the number of nodes, and p is the chance that any one arrow exists, with at most N(N − 1) arrows in total. If the graph meets the Asaf-Ferber condition, then Hamiltonian cycles must exist, and there are usually N!(p(1 + o(1)))^N of them. The Asaf-Ferber condition has two parts. First, every node must have at least one arrow coming in and at least one arrow going out. Second, p must be greater than log N / N.

A Hamiltonian cycle asks for more than simply being connected. This theorem describes the lowest level of connection a graph can have and still meet the condition, so it shows the minimum that can be achieved. If a group of nodes has more than one Hamiltonian cycle, it is very easy to make sure they are simply connected, as Figure 2 shows. If a subgraph of a directed graph contains enough Hamiltonian cycles, then switching on part of that subgraph can give several stable routes for waking up and recalling the whole subgraph. This fits very well with the original idea behind engram theory.

Figure 2

If a group of nodes contains several Hamiltonian cycles, then connected subgraphs can be formed easily.

So do real networks of nerve cells meet the conditions of this theorem? To answer this, we use a measure called unidirectional connection saturation to stand in for the chance of connection p between nodes in a random directed graph. Unidirectional connection saturation is defined in Equation 5, where M is the total number of arrows in the directed graph and N is the number of nodes in it. It describes, on a large scale, how well connected the whole set of nodes is. If a group of nodes has a high unidirectional connection saturation, then those nodes are better connected, and it is more likely that a path of connections exists between any two of them.

(5) (Saturate) unidirectional connection = M / (N(N − 1))

We then checked whether the directed graph made using Equation 4 (with k = 0.06 and λ = 41) meets the Asaf-Ferber condition. The detailed steps of the experiment are in the section "Supplementary material: Experiment on the Relationship Between the Average Unidirectional Connection Saturation of Directed Graph Subgraphs and Subgraph Size". Here is what we found.

Figure 3a shows the results for 80,000 directed graphs of different sizes, made using Equation 4. The horizontal axis shows the size of the group of nodes, and the vertical axis shows the average unidirectional connection saturation. Once the number of nodes goes above about 50, the average unidirectional connection saturation of groups of different sizes settles at around 0.033. With k and λ kept the same, it approaches a constant value. Figure 3b shows the curve y = log N / N. If we set log N / N < 0.033, then N > 152.29. Once N is above 1, log N / N keeps falling as N grows, while 0.033 stays the same. So, in theory, any group of 153 or more nodes makes the directed graph meet the Asaf-Ferber condition.

Figure 3

(a) The unidirectional connection saturation of directed graphs of different sizes gradually settles. (b) The curve y = log(n)/n compared with the saturation level we measured. (c) The share of directed graphs in which cycles form within two hops, for different numbers of relay nodes. (d) The number of Hamiltonian cycles in the group of nodes, as predicted by theory and as measured in experiments. (e) A sampling experiment showing a huge number of available connected subgraphs. (f) The cumulative share of subgraphs that are similar to each other, by more and more.

Using Equation 5, we can also work out how many Hamiltonian cycles there are when a group of nodes has 153 or more. Finding Hamiltonian cycles in directed graphs is an NP-complete problem, which means that the time needed to search for them grows extremely fast, roughly o(N!). For larger N, this makes it impossible to get an answer in a reasonable time. To get around this, we used a computer to list the Hamiltonian cycles in directed graphs with only a few nodes. For larger numbers of nodes, we used the Monte Carlo method, which estimates an answer by repeating a random process many times. The details of the experiment are in the section "Supplementary material: Counting Hamiltonian Cycles in Directed Graphs".

Figure 3d shows the overall results, and the values predicted by theory closely match the values we measured. This experiment shows that the subgraphs made by our model of how likely nerve cells are to be connected contain about as many Hamiltonian cycles as the Asaf-Ferber formula predicts. It also shows that the number of cycles in subgraphs of different sizes changes in a similar way. So, in theory, the directed graph model we propose has a large number of Hamiltonian cycles in its subgraphs, which makes it much easier to build connected subgraphs.

### 2.4. Connected subgraphs are fairly cheap to form

In a subgraph of a directed graph, cycles make the connections sturdier. They form closed loops that make sure all the relevant nodes are linked to each other, so each one can be woken up and can wake up the others. As we showed above, the subgraphs of our directed graph, which meet the conditions of the brain, contain a large number of Hamiltonian cycles in theory.

However, the brains of different people are not built in exactly the same way, especially at the small scale of the physical shape of the nerve circuits. Even so, they can still hold the same memories. This means that directed graphs with different fine details must be able to link nodes with similar meanings, such as nerve cells that stand for colours in the visual cortex or nerve cells that stand for sounds in the auditory cortex, along different physical routes.

At the same time, making connections costs something. There is a hardware cost linked to the length of the connections, and a cost in the time signals take to travel. So the connecting routes should not be too long. In graph theory, this can be measured in "hops", the number of arrows you must follow to get from one node to another. We tested in experiments (see the Supplementary material) how likely the first nodes to be switched on are to form cycles within two hops. The results are shown in Figure 3c.

We call relay nodes the in-between nodes that do not have to belong to the core group of nodes for an event. They can take part in short directed paths that help link nodes that are only weakly connected into a connected subgraph. With the chance of connection we used, we found that as long as there are enough relay nodes, the first nodes to be switched on can quickly be linked through nearby arrows, forming sturdy connected subgraphs.

We can also state this more precisely with mathematics. Suppose the chance of connection is given by Equation 4, and M nodes are spread out evenly. Then the expected distance between the nearest neighbouring nodes can be approximated as s. So the chance that this group of nodes fails to connect and splits into two separate branches (where M = M1 + M2) is:

(6) ∏(x = 1 to M1) (1 − P(be_connected) dx = J_s)^(M2), J ∈ {1, 2, 3, ..., M}

This is a product of exponential functions, and when M ≥ 20, the chance becomes very low. In the same way, if a failed connection splits the group into three separate branches (where M = M1 + M2 + M3), the chance is:

(7) ∏(x = 1 to M1) (1 − P(be_connected) dx = J1_s)^(M2) × ∏(x = 1 to M1) (1 − P(be_connected) dx = J2_s)^(M3) × ∏(x = 1 to M2) (1 − P(be_connected) dx = J3_s)^(M3), J1, J2, J3 ∈ {1, 2, 3, ..., M}

This value is also very small (see the Supplementary material for details). In the same way, we can work out the chance of forming even more separate branches. So the chance of successfully connecting a group of nodes of a given size is guaranteed.

### 2.5. The possible memory space is enormous

A directed graph with a large number of nodes has an extremely large number of subgraphs, because there are so many ways to choose groups of nodes. With the chance of connection described above, most of these subgraphs are likely to be connected. This means a directed graph can hold an immense amount of memory in theory.

Here is an example. In a directed graph with 540 nodes, if we pick 20% of the nodes to form connected subgraphs, the number of possible combinations is C(540, 108) ≈ 1.576 × 10^85. Suppose an event made up of 108 nodes is described by a sentence of six words. Then the theoretical limit of what the brain could hold would be equal to 1.17 × 10^77 volumes of the Encyclopedia Britannica. (We assume the encyclopedia is stored as text and images, about 6 GB, and that an average English word is eight letters long.)

We also know from Section 2.3 that any group of 153 or more nodes makes the directed graph meet the Asaf-Ferber condition, so it contains at least one Hamiltonian cycle. A group of 153 nodes could in theory produce about 2 × 10^269 different cycles. Even in a directed graph with a unidirectional connection saturation of only 3%, the Asaf-Ferber formula still gives about 2 × 10^36 Hamiltonian cycles, which is still an enormous number.

Hamiltonian cycles demand very strict connections, but in fact graphs that are only weakly connected can also carry memories. We cannot explore such a huge space within a limited time, so sampling is the only practical way to test it. In particular, we picked edges between these 153 nodes at random and checked whether they could form weak connections. Over a sampling experiment that ran without a break for 960 minutes, we collected more than 10^7 connected subgraphs, as Figure 3e shows. The number of connected subgraphs kept growing, and the slope did not start to level off. This shows that the directed graph as a whole has an immense possible memory space.

Memories need to be told apart, and the space of possible combinations is used only sparsely, so two subgraphs should be different enough from each other. If subgraph A and subgraph B have sets of edges, EdgeA and EdgeB, we define how similar the two subgraphs are by the share of their edges they have in common:

(8) Similar(A, B) = |(Edge)A ∩ (Edge)B| / |(Edge)A ∪ (Edge)B|

In words, this is the number of edges the two subgraphs share, divided by the number of edges they have in total, counting each edge only once. For the directed graph described above, we required that any two subgraphs be no more than 40% similar. The results, shown in Figure 3f, show that about 55% of the subgraphs meet this requirement. This greatly reduces the theoretical memory space, but it still leaves a large amount of space that can be used in practice.

### 2.6. Memories can be added one at a time

A directed graph can be seen as a stack of many connected subgraphs, each standing for a particular event through its own pattern of links (Hui, 2002; Wei and Luan, 2004). This is fundamentally different from current machine learning methods (like the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics and Chemistry). Those methods lump together a large number of very similar, uniform examples, learn from them all at once, and store what they learn as weights, which is basically a way of approximating a function. In our approach, the original examples can easily be pulled apart, and the approach is easier to understand.

Because new memories are added one at a time, directed graphs are better suited to this "record as it comes" way of working. Learning spread across the nodes inside the network can strengthen the pattern of links in each connected subgraph (Wei et al., 2023, 2024; Wei and Li, 2023).
